newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Government forces poised eight miles from Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Government forces poised eight miles from Kabul.

text.p: With the battlecry "God is greatest", elated troops of the ousted Afghan government fought their way to within eight miles (12 km) of Kabul by noon on Sunday, witnesses said.
They said government forces were pressing south along the old road which runs north out of the city to the Salang pass.

Reporters travelling with advance elements of former defemnce minister Ahmad Shah Masood's troops reached the town of Hussein Kot, which was taking occasionally heavy incoming mortar, rocket and artillery fire from their foes of the radical Taleban militia which captured Kabul three weeks ago.
Masood's troops were returning fire with truck-mounted multiple-barreled rocket launchers as well as howitzers.
Earlier, Masood's mainly Tajik forces sent rockets slamming into Kabul airport.

Reinforcements were streaming south, building up the mass of military force needed to sustain a counter-offensive which has brought Masood's men from their stronghold in the Panjsher Valley to the gates of Kabul in little more than a week.

No civilians were to be seen on the streets of Hussein Kot, which echoed with the sound of incoming and outgoing artillery fire. Rocket and artillery impacts sent plumes of dust and smoke spiralling skyward.
Most of Masood's men moving towards Kabul were infantry toting Kalashnikov rifles and rocket-propelled grenade launchers and laden with extra ammunition.
"God willing we will be in Kabul today or tomorrow," said Gul Haidar, Masood's front-line commander in Hhussein Kot.
"We are going without Dostum's men on this road. They will advance along the new road."
Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum sent his troops to reinforce Masood on Wednesday, cementing a military alliance between two northern commmanders who are rivals and sometime enemies.
A combined Masood-Dostum attack against Taleban forces on Friday evening broke the Taleban line near Bagram military airbase. Since then Masood's men have advanced more than 25 km (15 miles).

Dostum's forces were assembling just east of the Bagram junction for their push down the new road to Kabul. Tanks, truck-mounted rocket-launchers and several hundred men were gathered at the side of the road awaiting orders to advance.

If the ultra-conservative Islamic Taleban forces who hold Kabul face a determined two-pronged attack, with Masood pushing south on the old road and Dostum on the new road, Taleban's fighting strength will be tested as never before in their two-year-old rise to power.

Taleban still holds some of the high ground between the advancing government troops and Kabul, but those positions are under heavy artillery fire. Sporadic bombing attacks against government troops have had negligible impact.
Some Taleban troops appear to have been cut off from their lines by the rapid government advance and were offering stiff resistance on Sunday in the area between the old and new highways.

Masood's men have moved up so rapidly that the tail of his force is having a difficult time supplying the head. Men, weapons and ammunition were being ferried to the front by pick-up truck, army lorry and more than one private vehicle.

Shirin Agha, a Masood commander from Shir Khan next to Hussein Kot, was smiling in the wan October sun as he gazed up from the rampart of a destroyed mud fortification at the mass of Sultan mountain, the only barrier between his men and Kabul.

Shirin Agha led a tank and about 100 men back into his home village at dawn on Sunday and was awaiting orders to move forward again when the call to prayer sounded from his mosque a few hundred metres away.
"That is a beautiful sound to us," the commander said, staring across at the minaret from his perch on the top of a mud wall. "We are all Moslems here. We are going to Kabul."
"We started fighting yesterday morning at 10 o'clock and we fought until we got here at 6 o'clock this morning. Now we are resting before the final fight."
Not far away, the commander's truck-mounted multile-barreled rocket launcher unleashed a salvo, with flashes of light streaking off into the clear blue sky in the direction of Kabul.
"Those are headed to Kabul airport," he told reporters matter-of-factly.
"The Taleban are desperate to escape from us. But by tonight we will have a plan and we will be moving to the city."

As he spoke one of his soldiers on the wall, framed by the snow-capped peaks of the Salang pass in the distance to the north, mumbled "Allahu akbar, allahu akbar" (God is greatest, God is greatest), the battlecry of Afghan warriors.
